idiom_name: plain data object + external mapping metadata + generic mapper
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: keep the entity a plain data holder (fields, constructors, domain methods) that imports nothing persistence-specific, and put all mapping knowledge in metadata - a table/column declaration, an annotations or mapping file, a descriptor table - that one generic mapper reads per entity type. The mapper uses the metadata to build reads, inserts and updates and hands instances to a unit of work or repository, so no entity ever opens a connection, writes SQL or knows its table name. Cache or compile the parsed metadata once per type; leave the entity free of save/find/delete so the separation stays visible in the type.
code_sketch:
entity User { id, email }                        # domain state only
metadata users: { id -> User.id; email_address -> User.email }
mapper.load(User, key)      # generic engine reads the metadata
unit_of_work.register(user); unit_of_work.commit()
pitfalls: Leaving persistence helpers (save/find/delete) on the entity recreates the coupling the pattern removes.
Metadata that drifts from the schema fails at runtime; nothing checks it unless startup validation or code generation is added.
A useful mapping layer needs identity/change tracking and lazy loading neighbours - adopted alone it pushes the complexity into ad-hoc mapping code.
N+1 query problems arise from unoptimized lazy-loading of child collections: always profile generated SQL on relationship traversal.
Mass assignment (over-posting) vulnerability when external input is bound directly to entity properties without a permit-list.

Wrong move: bind an untrusted request directly to every entity property -> mass assignment can overwrite server-controlled fields and privilege flags -> instead map an allow-listed DTO or command and validate it before applying changes.
